case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 19-2-1998 passed by the High Court Division in Criminal Appeal No. 20 of 1992)
full_judgment:
KM Hasan J: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 19-2-1998 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division is Criminal Appeal No. 20 of 1992 allowing the appeal and sending it back to the trial Court for further investigation.

2. The facts, in short, are that one Jetindra Nath Paddar, Inspector, District Anti-Corruption Bureau, Satkhira, lodged a first information report on 31-8-1995 stating, inter alia, that the appellant filed a mutation case before the Upazila Revenue Officer, Satkhira, on 11-8-1984. He had also submitted a photostat certified copy of a decree of Title Suit No. 663 of 1978 of the Second Court of Munsif, Satkhira in support of his case. The appellant prayed for mutating his name in respect of 0.44 decimals of land in plot No. 1858 of SA Khatian No. 983 under 101 Kotia Mouza with Satkhira PS.

3. The Upazila Revenue Officer, having found from an information slip that the said decree was spurious and forged, rejected the said mutation case and forwarded the order sheets of the said mutation case to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Satkhira on 26-11-1984 for taking necessary action. The latter then issued a notice upon the appellant to submit his papers. On submission of the aforesaid certified copy of the decree of Title Suit No. 663 of 1978 the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) directed the Government Pleader, Satkhira to make an enquiry as to whether Title Suit No. 663 of 1978 was at all instituted. The Government Pleader, by his report, informed the Court that no such title suit was ever instituted and no certified copy of the said judgment and decree of the above suit were ever obtained from the Court of the District Judge, Khulna, and that the certified copy of the judgment and decree were all forged and fraudulent. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, referred the matter to the District Anti-Corruption Bureau to take necessary legal action against the persons involved in the forgery. Hence the Satkhira PS Case No. 50 dated 31-8-1985 was started by the District Inspector under sections 467, 468 and 471 of the Penal Code and charge- sheet No. 71 dated 30-7-1987 was submitted against the three accused persons including the appellant, under the aforesaid sections of the Penal Code and final report was submitted against Abdur Rahim and another accused person. At the trial, charges were framed under the aforesaid sections of the Penal Code, by the learned Additional District Magistrate, Satkhira.

4. The defence case is that since the appellant obtained an order of injunction against the Deputy Commissioner, (Revenue) in Title Suit No. 183 of 1985, the latter, by influencing the police, started the false case against the appellant, alleging that lie had used forged documents in the proceeding before a revenue Court.

5. The defence further claimed that because of the allegation of using forged documents in a proceeding before a revenue Court, investigation as well as the trial, ought to have been held by the same court, as per mandatory provisions of sections 195 and 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Since investigation as well as the trial was not held as per provisions of the aforesaid sections the appellant was entitled to be acquitted.

6. The Additional District Magistrate, Satkhira, who held the trial in GR Case No. 349 of 1985, by his judgment and order dated 11-11-1989 acquitted the appellant. Against which the State took Criminal Appeal No. 25 of 1990 before the Sessions Judge which was heard by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Satkhira, who by his judgment and order dated 9-6-1992 maintained the order of acquittal passed by the learned trial Court. The State then preferred Appeal No. 20 of 1992 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment, dated 19-2-1998 set aside the judgment of the courts below and sent back the case on remand to the trial Court, thirteen years after the proceeding was initiated. Against which leave was granted by this Division in a criminal petition for leave to appeal in following terms:

"Mr Syed Dastagir Hossain, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that when the allegation is that the petitioner using a forged document before the Revenue Court tried to mutate his name in the record of right, the proceeding as initiated is illegal. He submitted that in a case of such a nature there must be a complaint by the Court itself in accordance with the provision of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which is found totally absent in the present case. He further submitted that the High Court Division committed wrong and illegality in entertaining the appeal and disposing of the same on merit with a direction for sending the case to the trial Court for further investigation. He further submitted that when under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure there is no provision for second appeal, the High Court Division ought to have rejected the appeal in limini. "

7. Mr ASM Khalequzzaman, the learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant, submits that the certified copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 663 of 1978, having been used before the Upazila Revenue Officer in a judicial proceeding, no criminal proceeding could be initiated on a complaint lodged by the officer concerned under section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Thus, the basic requirement of law having been violated the appeal by the State before the High Court Division should not have been allowed and the case definitely 'should not have been sent back on remand to the appellate Court below.

8. Since a scrutiny of section 195 of the Code is necessary for deciding the legality of the impugned judgment the relevant portion is quoted below:

"Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure

(1) No Court shall take cognisance-

(a) 	...........

(b) 	. ..........

(c) of any offence described in section 463 or punishable under section 471, section 475 or section 476 of the same Code, when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any proceeding in any Court in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding, except on the complaint in writing of such Court, or of some other court to which such Court is subordinate.

(2) ……………………………………...

9. According to the section quoted above, a complaint in writing by the relevant court, that an offence specified in section 195(1) (c) of the Code has been committed in a proceeding before it, is necessary for any court to take cognisance of the offence. The learned Advocate for the appellant argues that even if the allegation, that a forged decree was produced before the revenue Court in the mutation case is found to be true, cognisance could be taken by a Court only on the complaint in writing made by the Court of the upazila revenue officer, before which the proceeding took place. In this particular case the revenue officer did not make the complaint. Therefore, the High Court Division failed to consider the implications of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and erred in allowing the appeal and remanding it to the trial Court.

10. This leads us to the pivotal question whether a revenue officer, dealing with a mutation proceeding, constitutes a court, as envisaged in section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Procedures followed in a mutation case are dealt with in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the Rules framed thereunder. Relevant rules" relating to mutation proceeding can be found in. Rules 23-24 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 which read as follows:

Rule 23 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955:

Duties of Revenue Officers-( I ) The Revenue Officer shall, if he is vested with necessary powers in this behalf under the Act, incorporate, and if he is not vested with such powers, send up proposals to the officer vested with such powers for incorporating necessary changes in the record-of-rights-

(a) When mutation of names is allowed as a result of inheritance either on the report of the Tahsilder under rule 22 or on the application of the heirs or otherwise;

(b) When mutation of names is made as a result of transfer on receipt of the notice of transfer under section 89 of the Act;

.........................................

…………………………

(2) Before sending any report under this Rule, the Revenue Officer shall satisfy himself about its correctness and for this purpose he may make such enquiries and take such evidence as he thinks fit. .

11. Rule 24 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955:

Duties of officers entrusted with the work of maintaining the record-of-rights: (I) Subject to the provision of sub-rule (2) the officer entrusted with the work of maintaining the record-of-rights shall promptly incorporate therein all changes reported to him under rule 23.

(2) Before incorporating any change in the record-of-rights, the officer shall carefully examine the report on the basis of which the change is to be made and shall satisfy himself about its correctness and for that purpose he shall follow such procedure and take such action as may be directed by the Board of Revenue.

<u>12. Rule 23 relates to duties of the Revenue Officers and rule 24 gives the duties of officers entrusted with the work of maintaining the record of rights. An analysis of the above rules will show that a mutation officer is not a court. The functions assigned to a revenue officer under the aforesaid rules, as to mutation cases, cannot be characterised as judicial functions, as he is not required by law to try a matter judicially and on legal evidence. The inquiry he makes and evidence he takes before sending his proposal is to satisfy himself as to the correctness of the report. It is more an administrative inquiry conducted for the purpose of maintaining an up to date record of rights for the state and to ascertain from among several claimants the genuine claimant, who can be given possession of the immovable property in dispute. In sum, its inquiry report lacks finality and authoritativeness of a court as the Revenue officers do not possess the power to decide the title to and the property rights in the immovable property. The decision of the Upazila Nirbahi Officer as to mutation can at least be considered as an executive order which is subject to final determination by a civil Court. (Similar view held in 6 BLD 7, 38 DLR 270 and 20 DLR J09).</u>

13. On perusal of the records it appears to us that appellant was charge sheeted for both cognizable and non-cognizable offences as the sections under which he is charge sheeted are sections 467, 468, and 471 of the Penal Code. Among these sections only section 471 of the Penal Code is covered by section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and others are not.

14. As we have observed above that the functions of a revenue officer in mutation proceedings are not judicial functions to make it a court, section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not attracted in this particular case. Therefore, in the instant case, a complaint in writing of a relevant court is not necessary and there is no bar in initiating legal proceeding against the accused appellant by a complaint lodged by a police officer.

15. The non-cognizable sections under which the appellant is charged with cause us to ponder, whether the permission from the Magistrate under section 155(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, should have been taken to investigate the case and record the statements of different persons under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, before submitting the charge-sheet against the appellant.

Section 155(2) reads as follows:

"No police officer shall investigate a non- cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case or (send) the same for trial.”

16. The question is, whether in the instant case investigation by the police into the non-cognizable offences under sections 468 and 471 without the sanction of the competent Magistrate has vitiated the proceeding taken by the court. To answer this, let us fall back on section 190(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and examine it.

17. Section 190(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure:

"Except as hereinafter provided, any Metropolitan Magistrate, District Magistrate or Sub-Divisional Magistrate and any other Magistrate specially empowered in this behalf, may take cognisance of any offence-

(a) Upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence;

(b) Upon a report in writing of such facts made by any police officer;

(c) Upon information received from any person other than a police-officer or upon his own knowledge or suspicions, that such offence has been committed."

<u>18. A scrutiny of the section shows that a report by a police officer, in respect of a non- cognizable offence, without being authorised by the Magistrate to investigate, will still come under clause (a) or (b) of section 190(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Such a report either could be held to fall within the purview of section 190(1) (b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure or may be accepted as a complaint under section 190(1)(a). The report, even if not recorded as a police report, may be accepted as a complaint within the meaning of section 190(1) (a) since it is a mere irregularity. An investigation by an officer not authorised to investigate a non-cognizable offence, in our view, is mere irregularity and does not affect the legality of the proceeding of a Court. There is also nothing in the law to prevent a police officer from making a complaint when some facts have come to his knowledge even if he cannot investigate them. In any case, no intention can be read into the law that the jurisdiction of the Court would itself be barred, when an unauthorised police officer conducted the investigation. The cognisance so taken is only in the nature of an error in a proceeding antecedent to the trial. A similar view has been taken in the cases of Abdur Noor alias Noor Miah vs State PLD, 1958 (Dacca) 145 = 9 DLR 312. The Crown vs Meher Ali, PLD 1956 (FC) 106 = 8 DLR (FC) 47; Sheikh Abdul Mazid vs State Delhi AIR 1955 SC 196, Siddique Ahmed and others vs State of 37 DLR 223 Golam Moula Master vs State 46 DLR 140.</u>

19. Moreover, section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is attracted in such a situation to rectify the irregularity, if any, Section 537 is to the effect;

"Subject to the provisions hereinbefore contained, no finding, sentence or order passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction shall be reversed or altered under Chapter XXVII or on appeal or revision on account-

(a) of any error, omission or irregularity in the complaint, summons, warrant, charge, proclamation, order, judgment or other proceedings before or during trial or in any inquiry or other proceedings under this Code."

20. since the decision of the Privy Council in the case of Abdur Rahman 31 CWN 271 (282) (PC) the consistent view of the courts of the sub- continent is that section 537 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in the absence of anything in the section itself to give it a restrictive meaning, may be taken to cover the error, omission or irregularity in the widest sense of these terms provided there has been no failure of justice. A similar view has been taken in the case of Madhya Pradesh vs Veereshwar Rao Agnihotri reported in AIR 1957 SC and Din Dayal Sharma vs State of UP the Respondent AIR 1959 SC 831 and 46 DLR 140.

21. In our view the investigation by a police officer in the instant case is neither the foundation-stone nor a prerequisite of the proceeding, nor a sine qua non of a valid trial in the Court. It is simply an antecedent proceeding and we don't see any reason why such an irregularity should be allowed to affect the proceeding or prevent the Court from taking cognizance of the offence under clause (a) or (b) of section 1990(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the absence of clear enactment expressed or implied, preventing the Court from doing so.

22. The next ground on which the leave has been granted is that no second appeal is allowed under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Therefore, the appeal before the High Court Division, which is, in fact, a second appeal, was not maintainable and the High Court Division should neither have allowed the appeal nor sent it back on remand. The language of the amended section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in this regard is very clear (substituted the original section by Ordinance, XLIX of 1978) and the learned Advocate for the appellant is quite right when he argues that the second appeal before the High Court Division was not maintainable.

23. But the fact remains that in the instant case, all the courts below have taken an erroneous view, regarding the nature of a mutation proceeding before the revenue officer, holding it to be a proceeding before a court on a misconception of law. An offence of serious nature has allegedly been committed by the appellant who IS said to have tampered, not only with the functions of a revenue officer, but also with the administration of justice by using a forged decree of a court. If the appellant is allowed to escape the due process of law on technical grounds, it will remain a blot on our legal system and injustice will be done to those who deserve justice. This should be viewed very sternly and discouraged to avoid repetition of foul play of this nature. It is a fit case where equity, judicial conscience and fairness demand that this court should exercise the plenary power it derives from Article 104 of the Constitution, to do complete justice.

The appeal is dismissed. However, the order of the High Court Division to send the case back on remand is maintained with some modification. In place of "further investigation" as directed by the High Court Division "further enquiry" is directed to be held.

End.
